strengths: The paper presents an intuitive and potentially useful continual-learning idea: learn lightweight mappings that reconstruct earlier latent spaces and compose these mappings at inference time. This separation between representation acquisition and retrospective correction is reasonably original, although related representation-alignment work is not examined deeply.

The method is described with equations, an algorithm, architectural details, and explicit task- and class-incremental inference procedures. The experiments cover CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet and report means with uncertainty.

The reported task-incremental results are promising when a large alignment set is available: with 5,000 previous-task samples, ILR reaches 82.05% on S-CIFAR100 and 72.50% on S-TinyImg. Table 3 also usefully explores current-task, previous-task, and generated alignment data.

The ablation over the cosine term and representation regularization is informative, and the paper openly acknowledges linear parameter growth, increasing chain latency, dependence on previous-task data, and difficulties in class-incremental inference.

The appendix provides optimizer settings, epoch counts, hyperparameter grids, rectifier architecture, hardware, and some GAN details. The societal-impact discussion appropriately notes privacy, bias, and misclassification risks, with no evident unresolved research-ethics issue.
weaknesses: The central empirical attribution is not established. All headline ILR results use nonzero alpha in Equation 4, which regularizes the evolving feature extractor using previous-task or generated samples and therefore directly modifies sequential learning. Table 5 shows that removing this term reduces S-CIFAR100 accuracy from 82.05% to 72.45% and S-TinyImg from 72.50% to 58.73%. There is no control using Equation 4 without rectifiers, so the experiments cannot determine whether the gains come from latent rectification or predominantly from one-task replay/distillation. This also conflicts with repeated claims that ILR does not change fine-tuning and requires no training modification.

The comparisons are materially resource-mismatched. Baselines receive buffers of 500 or 1,000 total samples across all past tasks, whereas the best ILR result uses 5,000 samples from the immediately preceding task. ILR's 5,000-sample setting is not compared against baselines with an equal data-memory budget. Parameter counts also omit stored images or latent targets, temporary copies of the previous backbone, inference FLOPs, and training cost. The GAN variant relies on an approximately 95M-parameter BigGAN, dwarfing the 11M-parameter backbone, but this cost is excluded from the comparison.

The class-incremental evidence is weak. ILR obtains 48.90% on S-CIFAR100 versus 51.83% for TAMiL and 51.13% for CLS-ER while using five times as many alignment samples as their buffers. The proposed averaging of separately normalized task-head probabilities is only loosely specified and is susceptible to cross-head calibration errors, as the authors acknowledge. Only one class-incremental dataset is evaluated.

Evaluation coverage is insufficient for the claims. The paper reports final average accuracy but not forgetting, backward transfer, per-task trajectories, chain-length degradation, wall-clock cost, training cost, inference latency, or memory in bytes. The PCA visualization is qualitative and no reconstruction-error measurement accompanies it. There is also no ablation of rectifier components or comparison with a direct/non-chained mapping.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript does not state the number of random seeds despite reporting deviations, provide code or pseudocode precise enough to reconstruct data flow and update scheduling, or specify several important implementation details. There are internal inconsistencies: Tiny ImageNet is described as 20 tasks in the main text but 10 tasks in the appendix, and the appendix reports an implausible 1,100,000 images while its stated train/test counts total 110,000.

The originality case is weakened by an outdated and category-level related-work discussion. For an ICML 2026 submission, the references and comparisons largely stop around 2023, and the manuscript does not carefully distinguish ILR from feature distillation, representation adapters, learned inverse mappings, or more recent continual-learning approaches.

Presentation is generally understandable but contains numerous typographical and terminology errors, including switching between ILR and LRB, incorrect dataset references in Section 4.3, and contradictory statements about whether the method changes training or uses replay-like data. These issues make the exact claimed contribution harder to assess.

Although the limitations discussion is commendably candid, it does not confront the most consequential validity issues: the dominance of Equation 4 in the reported gains, unequal memory budgets, and the omitted cost of generative alignment. Given these unresolved soundness and reproducibility problems, the promising idea is not yet supported strongly enough for acceptance.

strengths: Soundness: The proposed sequence of lightweight rectifiers is intuitive, equations and an algorithm describe its main mechanics, and the reported results include means with deviations, several baseline families, joint-training and fine-tuning references, and an ablation of the two loss weights.

Significance: Correcting representations after unconstrained task learning could be useful as a modular continual-learning strategy. The experiments span CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet, and the method performs competitively in some task-incremental settings.

Originality: Chaining transition-specific mappings backward through previously learned latent spaces is a distinctive formulation, even though its components closely resemble feature distillation, adapters, and dynamic network expansion.

Presentation: The manuscript provides helpful diagrams, parameter counts, alignment-set variants, and a candid limitations section discussing linear model growth, chain inference cost, dependence on previous-task data, and difficulty in class-incremental learning.

Ethics: No major unresolved ethical concern is apparent. The societal-impact discussion acknowledges bias, privacy, and misclassification risks, although it remains generic. weaknesses: Soundness: The strongest results do not isolate the claimed rectification mechanism. They use 5,000 previous-task examples both to train the rectifier and, through Equation 4, to regularize the main feature extractor. Removing this regularization drops accuracy from 94.84 to 89.68 on CIFAR-10, 82.05 to 72.45 on CIFAR-100, and 72.50 to 58.73 on Tiny ImageNet. A crucial baseline applying Equation 4 without rectifiers is missing, so much of the gain may come from ordinary old-data representation regularization rather than backward recall.

Soundness and fairness: ILR with 5,000 retained examples from the preceding task is compared against replay methods with only 500 or 1,000 examples total. Although ILR discards examples after the next transition, this is not an equal peak-memory, data-access, training-compute, or privacy budget. The paper reports only parameter counts—not stored latent targets, peak training memory, wall-clock/FLOPs, or inference cost—despite training extra modules for 50 epochs and evaluating through a growing rectifier chain.

Evidence: Evaluation relies almost entirely on final average accuracy. There are no per-task results, forgetting or forward-transfer measures, reconstruction-error measurements, chain-depth/error-accumulation analysis, timing results, or scaling experiments beyond at most ten tasks. The PCA visualization on CIFAR-10 is qualitative and does not establish that sequential compositions remain accurate.

Class-incremental evaluation is unconvincing. ILR uses separate task heads and averages their softmax outputs, whereas the comparability of this setup to standard single-head class-incremental baselines is not established. Even with 5,000 previous-task examples, it scores 48.90 on CIFAR-100, below TAMiL's 51.83 and CLS-ER's 51.13 using 1,000-buffer settings. Thus the evidence primarily supports a task-aware setting rather than general continual learning.

Reproducibility: The experimental description contains consequential contradictions. The main text says Tiny ImageNet has 20 tasks of 20 classes, which would exceed its 200 classes, while the appendix says 10 tasks; Table 4 nevertheless reports through 20 tasks. Section 4.2 says alignment sizes are 500, 100, and 5,000 although the table uses 1,000. The EWC search lists gamma in {0.9,1}, but Table 7 reports gamma=0.1. Table 4 also labels the method 'LRB.' The number of runs/seeds, batch sizes, task/class ordering, exact checkpoint-selection protocol, and code availability are absent.

Significance: Resource claims are overstated. Parameter growth is linear and reaches 21.96M at 20 tasks versus an 11.27M backbone; inference for old tasks traverses an increasingly long chain. The generative alternative requires a roughly 95M-parameter BigGAN per described setup, substantially weakening claims of compactness or practical data-free learning.

Originality and presentation: The paper does not sharply distinguish its contribution from adjacent feature-distillation, representation-alignment, adapter, and expandable-network methods. Claims such as requiring 'neither a replay buffer nor intricate training modifications' are misleading: the best variant temporarily retains substantial old data and explicitly modifies feature training through Equation 4. Numerous notation errors and grammatical issues further obscure the protocol. Overall, the central attribution and fairness problems are substantial enough to prevent reliable conclusions or acceptance in the present form.

strengths: Originality/significance: Incrementally learning lightweight maps from the current representation back to earlier representation spaces is an intuitive and reasonably novel continual-learning direction. Separating new-task adaptation from retrospective correction could make the framework easy to combine with other training pipelines.

Soundness: The method is concretely specified through the rectifier architecture, alignment objective, training algorithm, and task- and class-incremental inference procedures. Ablations indicate that both representation regularization and the cosine component improve accuracy.

Evidence: Experiments cover CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet, multiple replay and regularization baselines, several alignment-set sizes, and three alignment-data strategies. Results are promising, particularly the 82.05% task-incremental CIFAR-100 and 72.50% Tiny ImageNet results with 5,000 alignment samples.
Presentation: The central intuition and model diagrams are understandable, tables report uncertainty, and the appendix provides architectures, optimization settings, and hyperparameter grids.

Limitations/ethics: The paper candidly identifies linear parameter growth, increasing inference cost, dependence on previous-task data, and difficulties in class-incremental inference. Its brief societal-impact discussion acknowledges privacy, bias, and misclassification risks.
weaknesses: Soundness: The headline comparisons are not resource-matched. The strongest ILR results use 5,000 previous-task samples, whereas replay baselines receive buffers of at most 1,000 samples shared across all past tasks. At 1,000 samples, ILR is below CLS-ER on CIFAR-100 and below TAMiL on Tiny ImageNet. Consequently, the evidence does not establish superiority at comparable data budgets.

Reproducibility: The Tiny ImageNet protocol is materially inconsistent. Section 4.1 states 20 tasks with 20 classes each, which is impossible for the standard 200-class dataset, while Appendix A.2 states 10 tasks with 20 classes. The appendix also reports 1,100,000 images before giving the standard 100,000-training/10,000-test counts. These discrepancies leave the principal Tiny ImageNet results underspecified.

Resource accounting is incomplete. Parameter tables omit retained alignment samples, stored latent targets or the previous extractor needed during training, training cost, and inference FLOPs/latency. The generative variant relies on a roughly 95M-parameter BigGAN, far larger than the base model, undermining its presentation as an attractive memory-free alternative unless lifecycle costs are reported.

The class-incremental evaluation is insufficiently specified and narrow. It is unclear exactly how probabilities from disjoint task-specific heads are embedded and averaged, and only CIFAR-100 is evaluated. Comparability to standard single-head class-incremental baselines therefore cannot be confidently assessed.

The chaining mechanism lacks a decisive error-propagation study. PCA plots are qualitative and can obscure high-dimensional discrepancies; the paper should report reconstruction error and accuracy as functions of chain length, per-task performance, forgetting measures, and runtime scaling.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete: the number of random seeds is not stated, code availability is unclear, exact alignment-set sampling and latent-storage choices are not fully documented, and some baseline settings are described as having no hyperparameters despite optimizer and replay-related choices.

Presentation contains numerous consequential errors and imprecise claims, including switching between ILR and LRB, CLS-ER and CSL-ER, and incorrectly referring to the current-task alignment set as D_train^{t-1} in Section 4.3. Claims that ILR requires neither replay data nor training modification are also too broad because its best variant retains substantial previous-task data and Equation (4) explicitly modifies feature-extractor training.

The empirical scope is limited to small image-classification benchmarks and ResNet-18. Given the method's linear storage and chain-dependent inference, evidence on longer task sequences or a larger-scale setting is important for establishing practical significance.

strengths: Originality/significance: Retrospective feature estimation is an interesting perspective on continual learning. Mapping current features back through task-specific historical feature spaces separates new-task optimization from old-task recovery and could inspire useful follow-up work.

Soundness: The method, losses, training procedure, and task-/class-incremental inference rules are described coherently. Experiments cover three benchmarks, three seeds, multiple replay baselines, 10- and 20-task sequences, and both ResNet-18 and ViT backbones.

Empirical results: RFE is particularly competitive in task-incremental CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet. Without stored exemplars it reaches 79.54% and 69.66%, respectively, while RFE-P/B further improve several results. TinyImageNet class-incremental performance is also promising.

Analysis: The manuscript provides parameter counts, limited timing results, feature-reconstruction visualizations and RMSEs, alternative mapping designs, and an end-to-end variant. These analyses give some evidence that explicit feature rectification is useful.

Ethics: The experiments use standard public image benchmarks and raise no evident human-subject or deployment concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: The decisive mechanism is insufficiently isolated. Each retrospector contains an auxiliary encoder distilled on the preceding task, so RFE stores a compressed, task-specific model snapshot. The paper asserts that this encoder alone obtains below 53% on CIFAR-100 but supplies no controlled table, protocol, or comparisons against equally sized per-task adapters/encoders. Consequently, the evidence does not establish how much of the gain comes from retrospective mapping rather than dynamic capacity expansion and stored task-specific knowledge.

Soundness: There is no rigorous analysis of when mappings learned primarily from current-task inputs can recover previous-task representations, nor of error accumulation through a long chain. PCA plots and reconstruction RMSEs are descriptive; they do not establish class preservation, invertibility, or scaling beyond the evaluated sequences.

Comparison fairness: Most main baselines are replay methods, whereas the closest dynamic-architecture, parameter-isolation, and non-rehearsal methods are compared only indirectly using numbers from different papers, architectures, sample budgets, and protocols. This weakens the claimed advantage over existing continual-learning directions.

Evaluation: The strongest results are in task-incremental learning, where the correct task identity is supplied. In class-incremental learning, RFE is below CLS-ER on CIFAR-100, CIFAR-10 is omitted, and averaging separately normalized task-head probabilities lacks calibration analysis. Results are restricted to small image benchmarks with artificial class splits.

Resource claims need qualification. Exemplar-free RFE still retains a full previous backbone during training and accumulates 0.35M parameters per task at inference. Table 6 leaves several testing-time entries blank and reports only ten-task timing, so the assertion of moderate overhead does not substantiate scalability. Memory accounting also alternates between parameter counts and approximate image-to-parameter conversions rather than reporting actual peak memory.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance. The promised code URL after “Code is available at:” is empty. Batch sizes, replay minibatch ratios, class/task orders, precise sample-selection procedures for P, hardware, seeds, and several implementation details are absent. The hyperparameter searches are unusually narrow, including only alpha=1 for RFE, making the three-seed comparisons difficult to reproduce or audit.

The “data-free” and privacy framing is overstated. RFE does not retain raw exemplars, but its auxiliary networks and previous backbone are distilled from prior data and may encode or leak training examples. No privacy analysis or attack is performed, and temporary retention in RFE-P does not by itself establish a meaningful privacy guarantee.

Presentation has several correctable defects: Table 6 is incomplete, Section 4.2 repeats “RFE-P” where one instance should be RFE-B, and some appendix cross-references are ambiguous. More importantly, the limitations discussion omits the weak mechanism isolation, comparison mismatch, and unvalidated privacy claims.

Overall, the idea and results have clear merit, but missing decisive ablations, weak like-for-like comparisons, incomplete resource evidence, and insufficient reproducibility prevent others from reliably attributing or building on the contribution in its current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: The idea of correcting feature drift through a chain of learned backward mappings is intuitive and potentially useful, especially as a modular alternative to constraining every new-task update.

Soundness: The paper evaluates three variants across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet, includes both task- and class-incremental settings, reports three-seed variability, and provides a limited ViT experiment.

Empirical results: RFE is competitive in the easier task-incremental setting, with particularly strong results on CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet. The representation-error analysis also confirms that the modules reduce feature-space discrepancy.

Presentation: The method, architecture, training procedure, and resource-growth tradeoffs are generally understandable. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges task-identity dependence, linear parameter growth, chaining cost, and weaker CIFAR-10 performance. Ethics: The benchmark study presents no major immediate ethical risk, and retaining previous-task samples only temporarily could be useful in some applications.
weaknesses: Soundness: The experiments do not isolate the claimed retrospective mechanism from ordinary feature distillation and model expansion. Equation 7 already regularizes the current extractor toward the previous extractor, while every task adds an auxiliary extractor and mapping module. Essential baselines—feature distillation alone, the auxiliary extractor alone under matched capacity, and direct classification from stored auxiliary features—are absent. The paper dismisses some decompositions as impossible instead of measuring them, so the central causal claim is not established.

Evaluation fairness: The headline comparisons mix qualitatively different resources. RFE retains a complete previous backbone during training and accumulates task-specific parameters, whereas most baselines receive fixed exemplar buffers. Parameter counts and image storage are discussed separately, but there is no controlled comparison at matched persistent memory, training FLOPs, or inference latency. Claims of superiority therefore cannot be attributed confidently to the proposed mechanism rather than additional capacity and computation.

Baseline coverage/originality: Direct experiments concentrate on replay methods, although RFE is most naturally compared with non-rehearsal distillation, parameter-isolation, dynamic-expansion, feature-alignment, and backward-compatible-representation methods. Appendix B.6 substitutes cross-paper numbers obtained with different architectures, sample budgets, and protocols, which is not a reliable comparison. The limited engagement with closely related feature-translation ideas also weakens the claimed status as a new paradigm.

Significance: Most gains occur in task-incremental learning, where the true task identity and task-specific head are supplied at inference. In class-incremental learning, RFE is substantially below CLS-ER on CIFAR-100—for example, 43.63 for RFE and about 46 for buffered variants versus 56.18 for CLS-ER with 1,000 exemplars. The improvement on Tiny ImageNet is narrower, and CIFAR-10 CIL is omitted.

Class-incremental methodology: Averaging separately normalized task-head probabilities gives every task equal total probability mass and makes predictions depend on poorly calibrated cross-head confidence. No calibration study, task-identification accuracy, or comparison with standard single-head inference is provided. Referring to stronger task inference as future work leaves a central deployment setting unresolved.

Scalability: Parameters grow linearly with the number of tasks, while inference traverses an increasingly long chain. The evaluation reaches only 20 tasks, presents that experiment mainly as a curve without a full numerical comparison, and does not test large task counts or quantify accumulated mapping error against chain depth. This is insufficient to support broad continual-learning scalability claims.

Reproducibility/presentation: The promised code URL after “Code is available at:” is blank. Important details such as batch sizes, selected hyperparameters by dataset, class orders, random seeds, hardware, and complete timing methodology are missing. Algorithm 1 appears to swap the assignments of P and B, and Table 6 omits RFE-P and RFE-B testing times despite discussing them. These errors make independent reproduction unreliable.

Evidence breadth: Results are limited to small image-classification benchmarks, mostly one ResNet-18 protocol, average accuracy, and three runs. There is no direct forgetting/backward-transfer metric, statistical testing, robustness analysis, α sensitivity, task-order sensitivity, or study of distributionally dissimilar adjacent tasks—the condition under which training a backward map only on current-task samples is most questionable.

Ethics/limitations: The privacy discussion is too strong. Being exemplar-free does not make RFE privacy-preserving: retained teacher models and learned features can leak training information, while RFE-P explicitly stores samples and representations. No privacy threat model or empirical privacy evaluation supports the stated privacy advantages.

strengths: The retrospective feature-estimation idea is original and intuitively appealing: instead of only preventing representation drift, the method learns lightweight mappings that approximately reverse successive feature changes. Separating new-task learning from post-hoc feature rectification is a useful perspective for continual learning.

The empirical results are promising and reasonably broad. Experiments cover task- and class-incremental learning on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet, three memory configurations, chains of up to 20 tasks, and both ResNet-18 and ViT-S/16 backbones. In task-incremental learning, the data-free RFE variant is particularly competitive on CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet, while RFE-P/RFE-B produce strong results on longer sequences.

The representation analyses support the proposed mechanism rather than relying only on final accuracy: PCA visualizations and RMSE measurements consistently show rectified features moving substantially closer to their original representations. Alternative MLP mappings and end-to-end training are also evaluated.

Resource costs are reported more carefully than in many continual-learning papers. The manuscript distinguishes training and inference parameter counts, accounts for the temporary previous backbone, and provides training and inference times. Results are averaged over three seeds with uncertainty estimates.

The method, equations, training sequence, and inference procedures are generally presented clearly. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges linear parameter growth, increasing chain latency, weaker CIFAR-10 performance, and difficulty in class-incremental inference.

The work uses standard public vision benchmarks and presents no evident high-risk application. Its modular design could be practically useful because it makes relatively limited changes to the main task-training pipeline.
weaknesses: The principal comparison for the data-free claim is incomplete. Most controlled baselines are rehearsal methods, while non-rehearsal methods are discussed only through numbers imported from prior papers that use different architectures and memory budgets. A same-codebase comparison against strong regularization, parameter-isolation, and expansion methods is needed to establish that RFE is preferable to existing data-free alternatives.

The ablations do not fully isolate the source of improvement. There is no controlled auxiliary-extractor-only baseline, no direct no-auxiliary-feature version, and no component-wise study of the two gates, multiplicative fusion, projection dimension, or feature-distillation term. The assertion that components “cannot be easily decomposed” is not a sufficient substitute, especially because the method combines representation regularization with the retrospector.

Scalability remains only partially demonstrated. Every task adds a module, and inference traverses a task-dependent chain—or all domains in class-incremental learning—but timing is reported only for ten tasks. The 20-task experiment reports accuracy without memory or latency, and the evaluated sequences remain short relative to the setting in which linear growth is likely to matter.

The class-incremental evaluation needs stronger protocol justification. RFE averages separately normalized predictions from task-specific masked heads, whereas standard class-incremental baselines commonly use a globally normalized single head. The paper should establish that classifier structure and access to task partition information are comparable. RFE also trails CLS-ER substantially on CIFAR-100, so the class-incremental evidence is mixed rather than uniformly competitive.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for an unambiguous replication. The stated code link is blank, exact selected hyperparameters for each method/dataset, task class orders, and random seeds are not provided, and the implementation is assembled from several repositories. Algorithm 1 also appears to swap RFE-P and RFE-B when mapping the sets P and B to variants.

Some empirical claims are stronger than the evidence. Only three seeds are used, with no statistical testing; all methods are placed under a largely uniform Adam/40-epoch protocol that may not favor every baseline; and the experiments are limited to small image-classification benchmarks without distribution, domain, or architecture diversity beyond one supplementary pretrained ViT experiment.

The privacy discussion is too categorical. Deleting raw examples after one task may reduce retention, but stored previous models, representations, and auxiliary networks can still leak information. The paper offers no privacy analysis or formal guarantee, so RFE-P should be described as having a shorter raw-data lifetime rather than as a demonstrated privacy-preserving trade-off.

Presentation is generally strong but contains several correctable issues, including the swapped variant labels in Algorithm 1, repetition of “RFE-P” where RFE-B is apparently intended, incomplete per-variant timing entries in Table 6, and the missing code URL.
